A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MUC framework and Alignment Calibration method despite the changed title. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original unlearning experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MS-COCO using MoCo, SimCLR, and CLIP, including numerical comparisons, ablations, and alignment visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds SVHN results, larger-model evaluations, statistical tests, and supplementary analyses.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same objective: retain-set InfoNCE plus weighted negative-alignment calibration, positive-alignment calibration, and performance preservation. The weighting by unlearn-to-retain dataset size is unchanged. Expanded uniformity explanations and experiments with other backbones do not establish a revised unlearning algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 adds SVHN street-number images to the evaluated datasets (Table 6). CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MS-COCO remain covered. CIFAR-100 is moved from v1's appendix into v2's main text, rather than newly introduced.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparisons retain Retrain, Fine-Tune, Gradient Ascent, NegGrad, and l1-Sparsity. However, v2 removes Retrain's distribution from the negative-alignment comparison in Figure 2, where it appeared in v1. Retrain remains evaluated elsewhere.

E3.justification: v2 adds substantially different evaluation protocols: a deceptive encoder-substitution control, normalized average gap percentage, classifier-only evaluation with separately optimized hyperparameters, ResNet-50 accuracy evaluation, and resource measurements across ResNet-18 through ResNet-152. Section 5.5 also introduces a two-dimensional representation experiment. These additions do not establish changes to the retained training recipes in Appendix A.2.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained calibration ablations, v2 adds uniformity visualizations, utility sensitivity to alpha and beta, comparisons under alternative metric aggregation, and evaluation excluding unstable EMIA. It also adds deceptive-owner detection analyses, model-size resource analysis, and an AC-versus-Retrain heatmap discussed in relation to privacy. These address substantial questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: v1 already reports averages over five CIFAR trials and three CLIP trials, plus sample-level dispersion. v2 adds trial-level standard deviations in Table 13, identifies seeds 0–4 and their shared use across methods, and reports Gaussian-assumption t-tests and p-values in Tables 1 and 9. The existing trial counts are not reported as increased.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial SVHN, ResNet-50, normalized-gap, classifier-only, resource, and statistical results. It also revises existing entries: for CIFAR-10/MoCo with 50% forgetting, AC's EMIA changes from 48.64 to 55.02 and TA from 88.06 to 83.28, while the reported average gap remains 2.00 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 3). These are revised reported values, not demonstrated performance gains. The calibration-free ablation changes from 2.70 to 2.60, and the new classifier-only evaluation reports AC first or second depending on the setting.

T1.justification: Appendix B.3 introduces a mathematical definition of average gap percentage as the mean of metric-wise gaps divided by the corresponding Retrain values. This is a limited extension of the evaluation definitions. The AC objectives and existing forgetting-score and membership-inference definitions remain equivalent; neither version supplies unlearning guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain MUC, Alignment Calibration, approximation of retraining, and visually checkable black-box unlearning. The novelty framing receives a limited qualification: v2's introduction acknowledges prior contrastive unlearning by Wang et al. (2023) and distinguishes its contribution through comprehensive evaluation and baseline comparisons.

C2.justification: v2 explains performance preservation through representation uniformity and discusses EMIA's instability. It substantially expands limitations beyond v1's restriction to contrastive learning: no certified removal, random forgetting only, AC-specific evaluation tools, and testing only one deceptive-owner strategy. Appendix B.7 also acknowledges possible privacy leakage from visible unlearning traces and argues that practical risk depends on restricted adversary access.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository URL, SVHN dataset and split details, clarification that linear probing trains on retained data, and clarification of the encoder/projection-head notation. The resource experiment specifies four NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Wandb memory monitoring. Most optimizer settings, training budgets, and hyperparameter ranges in Appendix A.2 are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds explicit positioning against EncoderMU by Wang et al. (2023), additional LLM-unlearning citations, and references concerning pseudo-label or label-free unlearning and difficult removal cases. These extend the research context without replacing the paper's principal positioning. The newly cited methods are not thereby added as experimental baselines.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, parts of the introduction, and the problem-setting and evaluation exposition. Section 3 separates model-owner algorithm selection from data-owner checking into Sections 3.3 and 3.4. The title changes, encoder notation is standardized, and much of the terminology shifts from auditing to evaluation. These changes reorganize the central explanation beyond simply appending experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different publication layout and redraws Figure 1 around the two-party evaluation workflow. Figure 2 changes comparator display, ordering, and colors; the calibration ablation table is transposed; and CIFAR-100 tables move into the main text. New statistical and supplementary-result tables, uniformity plots, utility plots, and an AC-versus-Retrain heatmap substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves empirical transparency and scrutiny: Table 13 exposes variability hidden by v1's averages, Table 14 checks conclusions without unstable EMIA, and added utility/resource analyses and explicit limitations address important weaknesses. It also repairs the internally inconsistent CIFAR-10/MoCo 50% result block. Some new numerical inconsistencies remain, such as Gradient Ascent's CIFAR-100 RA being 62.66 in Table 4 but 62.56 in Table 13, and the statistical validation covers only one deceptive strategy. These shortcomings limit, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in assessability.
